title: Ramakrishna's snake: Brahman and Shakti
hookLine: is a snake lying still a different snake from the one that moves?
carry: brahman and shakti are one, still or moving
tomorrow: why is Shiva dancing in a ring of fire?

cards: Is a snake lying coiled in the sun a different snake from the one that slides off into the grass? Nobody would say so. Same snake, resting, then moving.
That small picture is credited to Sri Ramakrishna, the temple priest of Dakshineswar, and the year used it to open a whole stretch of teaching.
In the weeks after the Devi Mahatmya, the path stopped telling the goddess's stories for a while and asked what she is. Today's summit sit climbs back to that question: Shakti, as a way of thinking.

teach.h: SHAKTI: POWER, THE POWER TO MOVE.
teach.b: Shakti means power: the power to act, to make, to move.
In the teaching remembered from Ramakrishna, when the divine is thought of as still, beyond all doing, he called it Brahman.
When it is thought of as creating, keeping and dissolving the world, he called it Shakti, the Mother. Not two things: one snake, at rest and in motion. Now take that picture to a hymn the year read.
The Saundarya Lahari, a long poem to the goddess traditionally credited to Shankara, opens with a startling sentence.
In paraphrase: Shiva, joined with Shakti, is able to create; without her, the god cannot so much as stir. A hymn of praise that starts by saying the great god can't move a finger on his own.
That's the Shakta turn: power isn't a tool that someone holds. Power is the goddess herself. From up here, look how often the year came back to it.

The goddess rising out of the gods' own blazing power in the Devi Mahatmya, every weapon handed over to her. The Rig Veda hymn where a goddess speaks for herself: I move with the gods, I bend the bow.
The Lalita hymn that names the goddess as Shiva and Shakti in one form. Different texts, one thread: the world is not dead matter waiting for a spirit.
It moves, and the moving is divine.
Shakta and Shaiva teachers argue about how the two relate. But for a Shakta it changes an ordinary day: the busy, moving world, a kitchen, a commute, a body breathing, isn't a distraction from God.

how: Shakta devotees worship the goddess as the power that moves the world, reciting hymns such as the Saundarya Lahari and the Lalita Sahasranama, and calling her simply Mother.

o: a yoga pose held motionless at the end of a session
a look back from the top at Shakti, the power that moves
the climb to a hill shrine of the goddess

games.q: Shakti, from the top — tap the pairs.
p: a goddess speaking: I bend the bow

s: in Ramakrishna's picture, Brahman and Shakti are two different snakes
one snake: still, he called it Brahman; moving, Shakti, the Mother.
the Saundarya Lahari opens by saying Shiva can't stir without Shakti
joined with her he can create; without her, the hymn says, he can't even move.
Shakta and Shaiva teachers all describe Shiva and Shakti the same way
they read the relationship in different ways and argue about it.

games.q: you're writing a long hymn of praise to the goddess. how do you open it?
o: with her battles against the demons.
by saying the great god can't stir without her.
with a list of her temples.
games.why: the Saundarya Lahari opens that way: Shiva, joined with Shakti, can create; without her he cannot even move.

practice: Let the body settle until it's mostly still, then notice what is still moving: the breath, the pulse in your hands, small shifts of balance.
Don't stop any of it; let stillness and movement sit in one body, like the coiled snake and the moving snake, and if you pray, rest in the goddess as that movement.

wordCard.voice: The summit sit. One stretch of the year, seen from the top. Today's stretch: Shakti as a philosophy, and a snake that is the same snake, still or moving. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: śakti, power, the goddess as the power that moves the world.

carryVoice: Your line: brahman and shakti are one, still or moving. One snake, coiled or sliding off. See you tomorrow.
